page_contents_html:
Irritable bowel syndrome (IBS)

IBS is a disorder of gut-brain interaction. Make a positive diagnosis when symptoms meet Rome IV criteria, alarm features and relevant alternative diagnoses have been assessed, and first-line investigations are satisfactory.

Faecal calprotectin is not a routine test for every patient with possible IBS

Request it selectively when qFIT is negative, diarrhoea or loose stools persist, and inflammatory bowel disease remains a realistic differential. Do not use faecal calprotectin to investigate possible colorectal cancer.

This draft incorporates the NHS Scotland CfSD/Modernising Patient Pathways Programme IBS pathway published in January 2025.

accordion_sections.heading: Primary care assessment
accordion_sections.html:
Rome IV criteria

Diagnose IBS when there is recurrent abdominal pain, on average at least 1 day per week in the last 3 months, associated with at least 2 of:

  • Related to defaecation
  • A change in stool frequency
  • A change in stool form

Symptoms should have started at least 6 months before diagnosis. Bloating, urgency, mucus, incomplete evacuation and symptoms made worse by eating may support the diagnosis.

Look for alarm features and alternative diagnoses

  • Rectal bleeding
  • Unintentional weight loss
  • Abdominal or rectal mass
  • Anaemia
  • Frequent nocturnal symptoms
  • Family history of colorectal or ovarian cancer

Ask about family history of inflammatory bowel disease or coeliac disease, recent antibiotics or travel, medication, and features suggesting malabsorption. Examine the abdomen and perform rectal examination when clinically indicated.

New IBS-type symptoms in women aged 50 or over

If symptoms are new within the last 12 months, investigate for ovarian cancer in line with the current suspected-cancer pathway, including CA125 and pelvic ultrasound where indicated.

First-line investigations

  • FBC and CRP (or ESR/plasma viscosity)
  • Coeliac serology: tissue transglutaminase antibody with total IgA
  • TFT
  • Other routine bloods according to the presentation
  • Stool culture/testing if an infective cause is plausible
  • qFIT in line with the current lower gastrointestinal symptoms pathway

Do not delay investigation or referral for a suspected alternative diagnosis simply because symptoms also meet Rome IV criteria.

accordion_sections.heading: Faecal calprotectin - when to request
accordion_sections.html:
Use faecal calprotectin selectively

Consider faecal calprotectin only when all of the following apply:

  • There is persistent diarrhoea or loose stool and inflammatory bowel disease remains a realistic differential
  • qFIT is negative and colorectal cancer is not suspected
  • An infective cause has been considered and investigated where appropriate
  • The result will change management or the need for gastroenterology assessment

BSG guidance particularly supports faecal calprotectin in patients aged under 45 with diarrhoea where inflammatory bowel disease needs to be excluded.

Do not request routinely

  • For every patient who meets IBS criteria
  • For clear constipation-predominant IBS without features of inflammation
  • For stable, previously diagnosed IBS with no material change in symptoms
  • As a colorectal cancer test or instead of qFIT

Interpretation

Use the current NHS Dumfries & Galloway laboratory interpretive comment and local action thresholds. Infection and medicines including NSAIDs can raise faecal calprotectin; consider these before repeating or referring. Escalate a clearly raised result, or a persistently borderline result with compatible symptoms, through the chronic diarrhoea/inflammatory bowel disease pathway.

accordion_sections.heading: Primary care management
accordion_sections.html:
Explain the diagnosis, agree the main symptoms to target and provide planned follow-up. Signpost to NHS Inform: IBS.

Lifestyle and diet

  • Regular meals, adequate fluid and regular physical activity
  • Reduce excess caffeine, alcohol and fizzy drinks
  • Adjust fibre according to symptoms; soluble fibre such as oats or ispaghula is usually better tolerated than bran
  • Consider a 4-week probiotic trial and stop if there is no benefit
  • Refer to dietetics if symptoms persist despite general advice; exclusion diets, including low FODMAP, should be supervised by a clinician with dietary expertise

Medication according to the predominant symptom

  • Pain or bloating: consider an antispasmodic as required.
  • IBS-D: loperamide is the first-choice antimotility medicine. Titrate to a soft, formed stool (Bristol type 4).
  • IBS-C: consider a laxative, avoiding lactulose where possible. Linaclotide may be considered when optimal or maximum tolerated doses of previous laxatives have failed and constipation has been present for at least 12 months; review after 3 months.
  • Persistent pain: if laxatives, loperamide or antispasmodics have not helped, consider a low-dose tricyclic antidepressant. Start at the equivalent of amitriptyline 5-10 mg at night and titrate if needed, usually not above 30 mg. This is an off-label indication: discuss and document informed consent. Review after 4 weeks and then every 6-12 months.

Consider cognitive behavioural therapy, hypnotherapy or psychological therapy when symptoms remain refractory after 12 months of appropriate treatment.

accordion_sections.heading: Who to refer
accordion_sections.html:
Use the appropriate urgent or suspected-cancer pathway

Do not refer alarm features as routine IBS. Use the current lower gastrointestinal, ovarian or other relevant suspected-cancer pathway.

Refer to gastroenterology

  • Diagnostic doubt after appropriate primary care assessment
  • Abnormal investigations suggesting inflammatory bowel disease, coeliac disease or another gastrointestinal disorder
  • A clearly raised faecal calprotectin, or a persistently borderline result with compatible symptoms, using current local laboratory guidance
  • Severe or refractory symptoms with a major effect on physical or psychological health, work, education or daily function despite appropriate primary care and specialist AHP input
  • The patient requests specialist review after an informed discussion

Refer to dietetics or another specialist AHP

Persistent symptoms despite first-line advice should usually receive specialist dietary or other AHP input before medical gastroenterology referral, according to local service availability.

accordion_sections.heading: Who not to refer
accordion_sections.html:
Manage in primary care when:

  • Rome IV criteria are met, there are no alarm features and first-line investigations are satisfactory
  • Symptoms are stable or improving with explanation, dietary measures or first-line medication
  • There is established IBS with no significant change in symptoms or new alarm feature

Do not arrange routine colonoscopy, ultrasound, hydrogen breath testing or repeated inflammatory markers solely to reassure a patient with a secure positive diagnosis of IBS.

notes_for_editor: Major update: faecal calprotectin is no longer described as a routine test for all possible IBS; its use is restricted to ongoing diarrhoea with a negative qFIT where IBD remains a differential.
Numerical faecal calprotectin thresholds have deliberately not been hard-coded. Confirm the current D&G laboratory interpretive ranges before publication if numerical cut-offs are wanted.
Confirm the current local dietetic/AHP route and whether linaclotide has any additional local formulary restriction before publication.

The previous draft's blanket age >45 alarm criterion, ondansetron and prucalopride recommendations have been removed because they are not supported by the supplied national pathway/NICE core recommendations.
